mainTopic: Redeeming a captive who is a מומר, the ריש לקיש story, and the משנה about selling a field to a non-Jew, with the argument between רבה and רבי אלעזר over a non-Jew's ownership and מעשר
overview: The amud opens by finishing a story. A man who sold himself to the לודאי begs רבי אמי to redeem him. רבי אמי argues with a קל וחומר from a משנה that he should be redeemed because his life is in danger. The רבנן reply that he is a מומר who chooses forbidden food even when kosher food is in front of him, so רבי אמי sends him away. Next the גמרא tells how ריש לקיש sold himself to the לודאי, tricked them on his last day, and killed them all. Afterward he lived so simply that he regretted even the little saffron he left behind. A new משנה then rules that someone who sells his field to a non-Jew must buy its fruit and bring ביכורים, for תיקון העולם. In the גמרא, רבה and רבי אלעזר argue about whether a non-Jew's purchase in ארץ ישראל frees the produce from מעשר and whether it lets him dig in the ground. The disagreement turns on how each reads the word "דגנך". One proof for רבה, from the משנה in פאה, is pushed away, and one proof for רבי אלעזר, from a ברייתא, is pushed away by placing it in סוריא. A third proof, about a field owned by a Jew and a non-Jew in partnership, begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The captive begs to be redeemed
steps.stepSummary: The man who sold himself to the לודאי asks רבי אמי to redeem him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Redeem me!
steps.whatsHappening: The man finishes his plea to רבי אמי: 'Redeem me!' This sets up רבי אמי's response.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man had sold himself to captors who would likely kill him. Now he wants the Jewish community to buy back his freedom. The question is whether he deserves to be redeemed.

phrases.english: Redeem me!
phrases.notes: This is the end of a story that started on the previous daf: a man who sold himself to the לודאי came to רבי אמי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun on the previous daf.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Will רבי אמי redeem a man who sold himself into deadly captivity?

steps.title: רבי אמי proves he should be redeemed from a משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי cites a משנה: children of a man who sold himself are redeemed because of spiritual harm. So a man in danger of death should surely be redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We learned: One who sells himself and his children to non-Jews, we do not redeem him, but we do redeem the children, because of the harm. All the more so here, where there is a risk of being killed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי wants to redeem the man. He proves it from a משנה using a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the father is not redeemed, but his children are, so they do not become ruined among the non-Jews. If we redeem to prevent spiritual ruin, then we should surely redeem to prevent death. So even though this man sold himself, the danger to his life is a reason to redeem him.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sells himself (as a slave)
All the more so (a קל וחומר)

phrases.english: He said to him: We learned:
One who sells himself and his children to non-Jews –
we do not redeem him,
but we do redeem the children –
because of the harm,
phrases.notes: The worry is that the children would grow up lost among the non-Jews.

phrases.english: and all the more so here, where there is a risk of being killed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the man's plea with a ruling backed by a source.
steps.raayaObject: A man who sold himself into deadly captivity should be redeemed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה that children sold to non-Jews are redeemed because of spiritual harm, applied as a קל וחומר to danger of death.

steps.title: The רבנן object: he is a מומר
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say the man is a מומר, since he was seen eating נבילות and טריפות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said to רבי אמי: This man is a Jewish apostate, because they saw him eating unslaughtered carcasses and treif animals!
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן challenge רבי אמי's plan to redeem the man. They say he is a מומר, so the community should not redeem him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אמי's proof assumed the man is a regular Jew worth saving. The רבנן attack that assumption. If he openly eats forbidden meat, he has rejected the Torah, and the duty to redeem him does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: A Jew who has abandoned Torah observance (apostate)
Animals that died without kosher slaughter
Animals with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rabbi Ami:
This man is a Jewish apostate,
for they saw him
eating unslaughtered carcasses and treif animals!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אמי's ruling to redeem.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's decision to redeem the man
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A מומר is not redeemed. His eating forbidden meat shows he is a מומר.

steps.title: Maybe he only eats out of craving
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי suggests the man eats forbidden food לתיאבון, from craving, not to rebel.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Say that he eats it out of craving.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי defends his plan. He says the man may eat forbidden meat only because he gives in to his appetite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a difference between a מומר לתיאבון, who sins because he is tempted, and one who sins to rebel. Someone who sins from craving has not rejected the Torah, so he can still be redeemed.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אמי is not saying the eating is permitted. He is only saying it does not prove the man has thrown off the Torah.

phrases.english: He said to them: Say
that he eats it out of craving.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection that he is a מומר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Eating forbidden meat shows he is a מומר who is not redeemed.
steps.terutzMaskana: He may sin from craving only, so he is not a rebel and can be redeemed.

steps.title: He chooses forbidden food even when kosher food is there
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן reply that he sometimes passes over permitted food and eats forbidden food.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: But sometimes there is permitted and forbidden food in front of him, and he leaves the permitted and eats the forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן push back on רבי אמי's answer. Craving cannot explain why he would pick forbidden food over kosher food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he were only hungry, kosher food would satisfy him just as well. Choosing the forbidden food when both are available shows he sins on purpose. That makes him a real מומר, not just one who gives in to temptation.

phrases.english: They said to him: But there are times
when permitted and forbidden food are in front of him,
and he leaves the permitted and eats the forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the לתיאבון answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that he eats forbidden food only from craving
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Craving does not explain choosing forbidden food over equally available kosher food.

steps.title: רבי אמי sends the man away
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי tells the man to go, since the רבנן will not let him redeem him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Go, they do not let me redeem you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי accepts the רבנן's argument. He tells the man he cannot redeem him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once it is shown the man sins to rebel, he is treated as a מומר. The duty to redeem captives, even from danger of death, does not apply to him. The episode ends here.
steps.whatToRemember: A captive in danger of death is redeemed, even if he sold himself (קל וחומר from the children in the משנה). But a מומר who sins to rebel, not just from craving, is not redeemed.

phrases.english: He said to him: Go,
phrases.notes: Now רבי אמי is speaking to the captive, not to the רבנן.

phrases.english: they do not let me redeem you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי אמי accepts the objection and reverses his plan.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A מומר who sins to rebel is not redeemed, even from deadly captivity.

steps.title: ריש לקיש sells himself to the gladiators
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש sold himself to the לודאי, bringing a bag with a stone. He knew that on a captive's last day, his captors grant any request.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש sold himself to the gladiators. He took with him a bag and a round stone. He said: We have a tradition that on the last day, they do whatever he asks, so that he forgives them for his blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new, related story about ריש לקיש and the לודאי. This sets up what happens on his last day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the man in the last story, ריש לקיש goes in with a plan. He knows the captors grant a final request so the victim will forgive his death. He brings a bag and stone to use when that moment comes.

keyTerms.meaning: Gladiators, who used captives in deadly fights
A bag and a round stone

phrases.english: Reish Lakish sold himself to the gladiators,
he took with him a bag and a round stone,
he said: We have a tradition that on the last day,
phrases.notes: He means the captive's last day before they kill him.

phrases.english: whatever he asks of them, they do for him,
so that he will forgive them for his blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related story about selling oneself to the לודאי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש sold himself to the לודאי, planning to use the last-day request custom.

steps.title: ריש לקיש outsmarts his captors on the last day
steps.stepSummary: On the last day, the captors ask ריש לקיש what he wants. He asks to tie them up and hit each one a blow and a half, and he kills them all with one blow each.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the last day they asked him, 'What would you like?' He said, 'I want to tie you up, sit you down, and give each of you one and a half blows.' He tied them up and sat them down. Each man he struck with one blow died. He gnashed his teeth at the dead man and said, 'Are you laughing at me? You still owe me half a blow!' He killed all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The story from step 7 continues. ריש לקיש uses the 'last request' custom to tie up his captors and kill them with the stone in his bag.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 we learned the custom that captors grant any request on the last day, and that ריש לקיש brought a bag with a stone. Here we see why: his 'one and a half blows' request was a trick. He pretended each dead man was only laughing, so the others would not catch on.

keyTerms.meaning: He gnashed his teeth at him

phrases.english: On the last day they said to him:
What would please you?
phrases.notes: This is the custom from step 7: on a captive's last day, his captors grant whatever he asks.

phrases.english: He said to them: I want to tie you up and sit you down,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל חַד מִינַּיְיכוּ אֶמְחְיֵהּ חַיְיתָא וּפַלְגָא.
phrases.english: and strike each one of you one and a half blows.
He tied them up and sat them down.

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ כַּד מַחְיֵיהּ חַד חַיְיתָא
phrases.english: Each one of them, when he struck him one blow,
phrases.notes: He hit them with the stone inside the bag from step 7.

phrases.english: his soul left him (he died).
He gnashed his teeth at him and said to him:
Are you laughing at me?

phrases.aramaic: אַכַּתִּי פָּשׁ לָךְ גַּבַּי פַּלְגָא דְּחַיְיתָא.
phrases.english: You still have half a blow coming to you from me!
phrases.notes: He is acting, so the others think the dead man is just grinning and not dead.

phrases.english: He killed all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ריש לקיש story begun in step 7 and shows how his plan worked.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש used the last-request custom to defeat and kill all his captors.

steps.title: ריש לקיש returns home and lives with full trust
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש comes home and lives simply, telling his daughter his belly is his pillow. When he dies he leaves only a קב of saffron, and he still feels he left too much.
steps.simpleTranslation: He left and came home. He sat eating and drinking. His daughter said to him, 'Don't you want something to lie on?' He said, 'My daughter, my belly is my pillow.' When he died he left a קב of saffron, and he read this פסוק about himself: 'And they leave their wealth to others.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends by showing how ריש לקיש lived afterward. He spent what he earned and did not save for later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He took no money for comfort, not even a pillow. Leaving just a small amount of saffron still bothered him, so he read the פסוק about people who leave their wealth to others as a criticism of himself.

keyTerms.meaning: A קב (a small measure) of saffron
He read the פסוק about himself

steps.whatToRemember: The ריש לקיש story ends here. He was brave and clever in danger, and lived with such trust in ה׳ that he saved nothing for himself.

phrases.english: He left and came home; he sat eating and drinking.
His daughter said to him:
Don't you want something to lie on?
He said to her: My daughter, my belly is my pillow.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ שְׁבַק קַבָּא דְמוֹרִיקָא,
phrases.english: When he died, he left behind a קב of saffron,
and he read this verse about himself: "And they leave their wealth to others."
phrases.notes: תהלים 49:11

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ריש לקיש story after his escape in step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ריש לקיש lived with full trust in ה׳ and was troubled even by the small amount he left behind.

steps.title: משנה: selling a field to a non-Jew and ביכורים
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: a Jew who sells his field to a non-Jew must buy produce from it and bring ביכורים, because of תיקון העולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone sells his field to a non-Jew, he must buy fruit from it and bring ביכורים, for תיקון העולם.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic. The Jew who sold his field to a non-Jew still has to bring ביכורים from that field, and he must buy the fruit to do it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person brings ביכורים from his own field. Here the field now belongs to a non-Jew, yet the משנה makes the seller buy the fruit and bring ביכורים anyway. The reason given is תיקון העולם, a rule for the good of society.

keyTerms.meaning: First fruits brought to the בית המקדש
A rule made for the good of society

steps.confusionAlert: The seller does not bring fruit he still owns, because the field is sold. He has to buy the fruit from the non-Jew first.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who sells his field to a non-Jew
must buy and bring first fruits from it,
for the betterment of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the ריש לקיש story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller of his field to a non-Jew must buy produce from it and bring ביכורים, because of תיקון העולם.

steps.title: רבה: what a non-Jew owns in the Land of Israel
steps.stepSummary: רבה teaches that a non-Jew's purchase cannot remove the land's holiness or its מעשר obligation. But it does give him physical ownership, such as the right to dig pits and caves.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: A non-Jew's ownership in ארץ ישראל cannot free the land from מעשר, because the פסוק says 'For the land is Mine', meaning the holiness of the land is Mine. But a non-Jew does own land in ארץ ישראל enough to dig pits, ditches, and caves in it, because the פסוק says 'The heavens are the heavens of ה׳, but the earth He gave to people.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רבה's rule about a non-Jew who owns land in ארץ ישראל. It splits that ownership into two parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land's holiness belongs to ה׳, so a sale to a non-Jew cannot cancel the מעשר obligation. The physical ground can be owned by people, so the non-Jew may dig in it as an owner. Each half of the rule is backed by its own פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownership, the legal power of owning

steps.whyThisMatters: This two-part view of ownership (holiness stays, physical ownership passes) is the background for understanding how a non-Jew's field relates to מצוות of the land, like the ביכורים in the משנה.

phrases.english: Gemara: Rabba says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין קִנְיָן לְגוֹי בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: Even though a non-Jew has no ownership in the Land of Israel
strong enough to remove it from the obligation of tithes,
as it is stated: "For the land is Mine,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:23

phrases.english: meaning: the holiness of the land is Mine;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל יֵשׁ קִנְיָן לְגוֹי בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: but a non-Jew does have ownership in the Land of Israel
to dig in it pits, ditches, and caves,
as it is stated: "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord,
but the earth He has given to the children of men."
phrases.notes: תהלים 115:16

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין קִנְיָן לְגוֹי בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה by defining what a non-Jew's ownership of land in ארץ ישראל means.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A non-Jew's purchase does not remove the land's holiness or its מעשר obligation, but it does give him physical ownership, such as the right to dig.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר holds the exact opposite of רבה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says a non-Jew's purchase does free the land's produce from מעשר, based on "דגנך". It does not give him the right to dig pits, ditches and caves, because "לה׳ הארץ".
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: A non-Jew's purchase in ארץ ישראל is strong enough to free the land from מעשר, because the פסוק says "your grain", and not a non-Jew's grain. But it is not strong enough to let him dig pits, ditches and caves there, because the פסוק says "The land belongs to ה׳."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי אלעזר, who flips both halves of רבה's rule from step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה said the purchase does not remove מעשר but does give physical rights like digging. רבי אלעזר says the reverse: the purchase removes מעשר, but there are no digging rights. Each half of his view has its own פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownership, the legal power a purchase gives
To remove or cancel (here, to cancel the מעשר obligation)
"Your grain", the word in the פסוק about מעשר
Pits, ditches, and caves dug into the ground

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two views. רבה: מעשר stays, but he may dig. רבי אלעזר: no מעשר, but he may not dig. They are exact opposites.

phrases.english: And רבי אלעזר says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ קִנְיָן לְגוֹי
phrases.english: Even though a non-Jew has ownership
in ארץ ישראל to remove the land from the obligation of tithes,
as it says: "your grain", and not a non-Jew's grain;
phrases.notes: דברים 12:17

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֵין קִנְיָן לְגוֹי בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: but a non-Jew does not have ownership in ארץ ישראל
to dig in it pits, ditches, and caves,
as it says: "The land belongs to ה׳."
phrases.notes: תהלים 24:1

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the opposing view to רבה's rule in step 11
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A non-Jew's purchase removes the מעשר obligation, but gives him no right to dig pits, ditches and caves.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבה and רבי אלעזר really disagree about. It answers that they read "דגנך" differently: either as grain from a Jew's land, or as grain a Jew piled up.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are they arguing about? One Sage holds that "your grain" means grain from your land, not a non-Jew's grain. The other Sage holds it means "your piling" of the grain, not a non-Jew's piling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the root of the argument, and then explains that it comes down to how each one reads the word "דגנך".
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר reads "דגנך" as grain from a Jew's land, so a field a non-Jew owns is exempt. רבה reads it as "דיגונך", the piling-up of the grain, which is what triggers מעשר. So what matters is who piles it up, not who owns the land. That is why the purchase alone does not remove מעשר for רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Your piling-up of the grain into a heap

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבה does not ignore the word "דגנך". He simply reads it as being about the act of piling, not about land ownership.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?
One Sage holds: "your grain", and not a non-Jew's grain,
phrases.notes: This first Sage is רבי אלעזר.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: דִּיגּוּנְךָ, וְלֹא דִּיגּוּן גּוֹי.
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: your piling, and not a non-Jew's piling.
phrases.notes: This is רבה. He reads the word as the piling-up of grain into a heap.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the two opposing views
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What principle splits רבה and רבי אלעזר?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They read "דגנך" differently: as grain from a Jew's land (רבי אלעזר), or as grain a Jew piled up (רבה).

steps.title: רבה brings a proof from a משנה about a non-Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה
steps.stepSummary: רבה cites a משנה: a non-Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה must be tithed, unless he made them ownerless.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: How do I know this? We learned in a משנה: The gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner produce of a non-Jew must be tithed, unless he made them ownerless.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה brings a משנה to support his view. The גמרא will next work out what case it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה wants to show that a non-Jew owning the land does not cancel מעשר. The משנה says a non-Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה must be tithed. If that is talking about his own field, it supports רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do I say this? (introduces a proof)
As we learned in a משנה
Gleanings: stalks that fall during harvest, left for the poor
Sheaves forgotten in the field, left for the poor
The corner of the field, left for the poor

phrases.english: רבה said: From where do I say this?
phrases.notes: He means his rule from before: a non-Jew's purchase doesn't remove מעשר.

phrases.english: As we learned in a משנה:
phrases.notes: פאה 4:9

phrases.english: The gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner produce of a non-Jew
are obligated in tithes,
unless he made them ownerless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבה's view and offers support for it
steps.raayaObject: רבה's rule that a non-Jew's purchase does not remove the מעשר obligation
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in פאה: a non-Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה must be tithed unless he made them ownerless

steps.title: The משנה cannot mean a Jew's field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה means. It rules out a Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה collected by a non-Jew, because those are already ownerless.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it means a Jew's gleanings that a non-Jew collected, why would it say "unless he made them ownerless"? They are already ownerless!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what case the משנה is talking about, and rejects the first possible answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה are ownerless by Torah law, since anyone poor may take them. So the phrase "unless he made them ownerless" makes no sense for them. That reading of the משנה cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?
If you say (offers a possible reading, often to reject it)

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say it is a Jew's, and a non-Jew collected them,
then why "unless he made them ownerless"?!
But they are already ownerless!
phrases.notes: Gleanings, forgotten sheaves and corner produce of a Jew already belong to no one; any poor person may take them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the case of the משנה by rejecting one possible reading
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading the משנה as a Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה collected by a non-Jew
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה are already ownerless, so "unless he made them ownerless" would mean nothing.

steps.title: So the משנה must mean a non-Jew's field, collected by a Jew
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes the משנה must mean a non-Jew's own field, with a Jew collecting the produce. This is the case that will support רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it talking about a non-Jew's produce, and a Jew collected it?
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected the first reading, the גמרא offers the only reading left: the field belongs to a non-Jew, and a Jew gathered the produce. The proof keeps going in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the field is the non-Jew's own, so his purchase is what is being tested. Since the משנה still requires tithes when a Jew collects the produce, the גמרא is heading toward showing that the non-Jew's ownership did not cancel מעשר, which is רבה's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't it...? (introduces the reading that must be right)

phrases.english: Rather, isn't it a non-Jew's,
and a Jew collected them;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the first reading, offers the reading that supports רבה
steps.raayaObject: רבה's rule that a non-Jew's ownership does not remove the מעשר obligation
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה, read as a non-Jew's field whose לקט, שכחה and פאה a Jew collected

steps.title: The inference: only making it ownerless frees it
steps.stepSummary: The משנה only frees the produce because the non-Jew made it ownerless. So if he had not, it would need מעשר, which means his ownership of the field did not free it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The only reason it is free from tithes is that he made it ownerless. If he had not made it ownerless, it would be obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof for רבה. It reads the משנה closely: the produce is free from מעשר only because of הפקר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 16 the גמרא set up the case as a non-Jew's own field, with a Jew collecting the produce. Here it adds the key point: the only thing that frees the produce is that the non-Jew made it ownerless. So the non-Jew's ownership alone does not free the produce from מעשר, which is what רבה holds.

phrases.english: The reason is that he made it ownerless,
but if he did not make it ownerless, it is obligated!
phrases.notes: So the field itself, even though a non-Jew owns it, still carries the obligation of מעשר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that step 16 set up.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's view that a non-Jew's purchase does not free the land's produce from מעשר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A close reading of the משנה: only הפקר frees a non-Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה.

steps.title: It could be a Jew's field after all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The משנה can be about a Jew's field whose לקט, שכחה and פאה a non-Jew collected. The Jew only made them ownerless for poor Jews, not for a non-Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really, it is a Jew's produce and a non-Jew collected it. And as for what you said, that it is already ownerless: granted he made it ownerless for a Jew, but did he make it ownerless for a non-Jew?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רבה's proof. It goes back to the case it ruled out in step 15 and shows that the case works after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 15 the objection was that a Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה are already ownerless, so the משנה's words "unless he made them ownerless" would make no sense. The answer: the owner gives them up only for a Jew to take. When a non-Jew takes them, they were never ownerless for him, so they still need מעשר. Now the משנה says nothing about a non-Jew's field, and the proof for רבה is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in fact (going back to an earlier option)
With the intention of, for the sake of

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think a Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה are ownerless for everyone. The point here is that the owner gives them up only for a Jew, so for a non-Jew they were never ownerless.

phrases.english: No, really, it is a Jew's [produce]
and a non-Jew collected it,
and as for what you said: "But they are already ownerless,"
granted that they are made ownerless with a Jew in mind,
are they made ownerless with a non-Jew in mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of steps 16 and 17 by bringing back the case ruled out in step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof for רבה from this משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed a Jew's לקט, שכחה and פאה are ownerless even for a non-Jew. They are ownerless only for Jews.

steps.title: A field that reached a third in a Jew's hands
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a Jew bought a field from a non-Jew before the crop reached a third of its growth, then sold it back after. The crop must be tithed because it already became obligated. The inference: had it not become obligated in the Jew's hands, it would be free, which supports רבי אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A Jew bought a field from a non-Jew before it reached a third of its growth, and then sold it back to him after it reached a third. It must be tithed, because it already became obligated. If it became obligated, yes; if it did not become obligated, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to prove רבי אלעזר right, against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reaching a third of its growth is the stage when the crop becomes obligated in מעשר. The ברייתא gives the reason for tithing as "it already became obligated" while the Jew owned it. That suggests a crop that reached a third while a non-Jew owned the field would be free, so a non-Jew's ownership does free the produce from מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source as a proof)
A third of the crop's full growth

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A Jew who bought a field from a non-Jew
before it reached a third [of its growth],
and then sold it back to him
phrases.notes: "To him" means back to the same non-Jew.

phrases.english: after it reached a third –
it is obligated in tithes, because it already became obligated.
If it became obligated – yes,
if it did not become obligated – no!
phrases.notes: So a crop that reached a third while the non-Jew owned the field would be free from מעשר.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלָּקַח שָׂדֶה מִגּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof for רבה was pushed away, the גמרא brings a source that leans the other way.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's view that a non-Jew's purchase frees the land's produce from מעשר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a field bought from and sold back to a non-Jew, read with the inference "if it did not become obligated, no."

steps.title: The case is in סוריא, which is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away the proof. The ברייתא is talking about סוריא, and its author holds that a conquest by an individual does not count as a real conquest. So we learn nothing about ארץ ישראל itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? In סוריא, and he holds that the conquest of an individual is not called a conquest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the proof from step 19 by putting the ברייתא in a special place, סוריא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סוריא was conquered by דוד on his own, not by the whole Jewish people together. The author of the ברייתא holds that such a conquest does not give the land the full holiness of ארץ ישראל, so there a non-Jew's ownership can free the crop. In ארץ ישראל itself, רבה can still say a non-Jew's purchase does not free the produce from מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (limits a source to a special case)
Syria, land conquered outside the main borders of ארץ ישראל
A conquest by one person, not by the whole nation together

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs failed. The משנה can be about a Jew's field, and the ברייתא can be about סוריא. So the argument between רבה and רבי אלעזר still stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that rules about the holiness of the land can differ between ארץ ישראל itself and lands like סוריא, so a source about one place may not teach about the other.

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here –
in Syria,
and he holds: the conquest of an individual
is not called a conquest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof for רבי אלעזר from this ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ברייתא is about ארץ ישראל itself. It is about סוריא, where the land's holiness is weaker.

steps.title: A new proof begins: a Jew and a non-Jew who bought a field together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a new proof from a ברייתא about a Jew and a non-Jew who bought a field as partners. Only the case is stated here. The ruling follows next.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear a proof: A Jew and a non-Jew who bought a field together as partners...
steps.whatsHappening: The previous proof was pushed away, so the גמרא brings a new source. This line only sets up the case. The ruling, and the proof built on it, come on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier proofs dealt with a field owned by one person, either a Jew or a non-Jew. This ברייתא tests a field owned by both at once. That is a fresh way to ask whether the non-Jew's share of ownership affects the obligation of מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: "Come and hear": the opening words the גמרא uses to bring a source as a proof

steps.confusionAlert: Do not decide yet whose side this proof supports. The ברייתא's ruling is quoted on the next amud.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A Jew and a non-Jew
who bought a field in partnership,

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹי שֶׁלָּקְחוּ שָׂדֶה בְּשׁוּתָּפוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof in Step 19 was pushed away in Step 20, the גמרא brings a new source to try again.
steps.raayaObject: The debate between רבה and רבי אלעזר over whether a non-Jew's ownership of land in ארץ ישראל frees the crops from מעשר
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a field jointly bought by a Jew and a non-Jew. Only the case is given so far.
